statement: In how many ways can $8$ identical cookies be shared among $3$ children so that each child gets at least $2$ cookies?

choices.misconception: I gave each child 2 cookies and then thought the 2 leftover cookies had to go to the same child, which gives 3 ways.
I gave out the 6 required cookies but then used C(2 + 3, 3) = 10 for the 2 leftover cookies, with one too many in the top.
I only made sure each child got at least 1 cookie, which gives C(7, 2) = 21, instead of at least 2.
I ignored the at-least-2 rule and used C(8 + 2, 2) = 45, the count when a child may get no cookies.

hints: Hand out the required cookies first.
After each child gets 2, the rest can be shared with no restriction. Sharing identical items among children with zeros allowed is stars and bars.
After giving $2$ each, $2$ cookies remain for $3$ children: $\binom{2 + 2}{2}$ ways.

solutions.reliable: Give each child $2$ cookies first; that uses $6$, and every valid sharing starts this way. Now share the remaining $2$ identical cookies among $3$ children with no restriction. By stars and bars, that is $\binom{2 + 3 - 1}{3 - 1} = \binom{4}{2} = 6$. Listing confirms it: the leftover split is one of $(2,0,0)$ in $3$ orders or $(1,1,0)$ in $3$ orders, $6$ in all. Transferable idea: a lower bound on each box is handled by pre-filling the boxes.

author: Devansh Sanghavi
